narrative:
The model estimates a 64% chance that you will leave your job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key factors that, in combination, signal a higher risk of departure compared to colleagues who are expected to stay.

The strongest influence is that you have received other job opportunities while at your current company. Unlike most employees predicted to stay—77% of whom report no such offers—this stands out as the top reason pushing the prediction toward leaving, as external options often make people more likely to move on.

Next, your difficult work-life balance contributes significantly to the "will leave" outcome. While only 9% of stayers report a difficult balance, this challenge for you adds notable weight toward predicting departure, as it suggests ongoing strain that could lead to burnout or dissatisfaction over time.

Your 6-10 years of overall experience also plays an important role, though it pulls in the opposite direction. This level of experience is more common among those expected to stay (35% of stayers) than very junior profiles, slightly encouraging the model to think you might remain. However, it is not enough to outweigh the stronger influences from opportunities and work-life imbalance.

The organization should discuss ways to improve your work-life balance and explore how to make staying more appealing than external offers. You may want to reflect on whether better support in these areas could change your plans. (248 words)
